topic: Missouri's two maps — a state injunction, a federal restraining order, and a secretary of state facing contempt this morning
question: Which congressional map is legally in effect in Missouri on November 3 — and did the secretary of state have a lawful choice when he picked one?
summary:
At 10 a.m. Central today, Missouri Secretary of State Denny Hoskins must appear before the Missouri Supreme Court and explain why he should not be held in contempt. Nine days ago the question was academic; now it decides one House seat and, plausibly, the chamber.

On September 3 the Missouri Supreme Court held that a referendum petition filed in December 2025 suspended HB 1, the mid-decade map the legislature passed at the president's urging. The court's conclusion was categorical: HB 1 'never took effect,' and the 2022 districts — six Republican, two Democratic — govern in November. On September 8 Justice Brett Kavanaugh refused to stay that ruling. Minutes later, Chief U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark ordered Missouri to use HB 1 anyway, holding that voters who chose nominees in an August primary run under those lines may not be moved. Hoskins emailed county clerks to use HB 1, citing the Supremacy Clause. The referendum's backers moved for contempt, and separately asked the U.S. Supreme Court to vacate Clark's order.

One map elects a seventh Republican; the other does not. Military ballots must go out September 19. The meter cannot say which map should govern — but it can check what each side says the law and the record contain.
verdict: The left's checkable case is the stronger one today, and rests mainly on documents its opponents wrote or lost: a unanimous state high court — five of its seven judges appointed by Republican governors — reading its own constitution's plain text, backed by U.S. Supreme Court precedent from 1916 and 2023 that squarely rejects the Elections Clause theory Missouri revives. The right's best facts are real and underweighted by its critics: 1.2 million people did vote under HB 1, no court has ever swapped maps between a primary and a general, and the September 19 federal ballot deadline is genuine. Which map deserves to govern is not something evidence settles.
verificationNote: Almost every claim here was read in a primary document: the Missouri Supreme Court's September 3 opinion, the Secretary's emergency application and von Glahn's opposition from the U.S. Supreme Court's own docket in No. 26A304, the docket entry recording Kavanaugh's denial, Moore v. Harper's slip opinion, and 52 U.S.C. § 20302. Judge Clark's temporary restraining order was not directly readable; its operative language is taken from four outlets that quote it, and is marked medium confidence. Missouri Independent, Election Law Blog, Ballotpedia and CNN returned 403 or 451 and were not used as sources.
sources_consulted: Missouri Supreme Court, von Glahn v. Hoskins (SC101805)

left.label: A law that never took effect cannot be the map
left.framing: Missouri's constitution lets voters suspend any act of the legislature by petition, and 300,000 of them did. The state's own high court said so unanimously. A single federal district judge cannot tell Missouri what its constitution means, and the calendar emergency was built by the official now invoking it.
left.strongestPoint: The documents belong to the other side. The Missouri Supreme Court found the secretary sat on the petition until the last legal hour despite being warned in December 2025, and his own attorney general had said on the radio that 'delay works in our favor.' On the federal question, Moore v. Harper decided this in 2023, with Kavanaugh in the majority.
left.weakestPoint: 'Defiance' overstates it. Hoskins faced two orders that command opposite acts, and calling that simple lawlessness skips the conflict. And 1.2 million people really did vote in districts that would now vanish — a cost the left mostly waves away as the state's own fault, which explains it without answering it.

right.label: You cannot change the map after the primary
right.framing: Missourians nominated candidates in August under HB 1. Swapping maps eight weeks later voids that election, blows the federal deadline for military ballots, and lets 3.3% of registered voters suspend a map their legislature passed. A federal court has now ordered otherwise, and the Supremacy Clause is not optional.
right.strongestPoint: The unprecedentedness is real and conceded by nobody's opponent: no court has previously ordered a congressional map changed between a completed primary and the general. UOCAVA's 45-day rule is a statute, not a talking point, and September 19 is nine days out. Missouri's brief also candidly admits the Court has never applied Purcell to a state court's own election ruling.
right.weakestPoint: The emergency is self-inflicted, on a record the state made. The secretary was told in December 2025 that he could settle HB 1's status early, chose full signature verification and the last permitted day, and ran the primary on a map whose legal status was openly unresolved. The 'impossible' finding traces to one affidavit from a former official.

facts.claim: Under Missouri law HB 1 never took effect, and the 2022 congressional districts are the only map in force for November.
facts.evidence: Opinion: 'Because the referendum petition was legal, sufficient, and timely, HB 1 never took effect and was referred to the voters as of December 9, 2025. The congressional districts the General Assembly established in 2022 remain in full force and effect for the November 2026 general election.' Signed by Judge Gooch: 'All concur.'
facts.explanation: This is a state high court's construction of its own constitution, which federal courts ordinarily accept as conclusive. It is not a finding about what is administratively achievable, and the court expressly declined to reach the federal objections, treating them as outside the secretary's statutory review.
facts.source: Missouri Supreme Court, von Glahn v. Hoskins, No. SC101805 (Sept. 3, 2026)

facts.claim: The U.S. Constitution's Elections Clause forbids a state referendum from suspending a congressional map the legislature enacted.
facts.evidence: Moore v. Harper: 'We hold that it does not. The Elections Clause does not insulate state legislatures from the ordinary exercise of state judicial review.' The Court there reaffirmed Ohio ex rel. Davis v. Hildebrant (1916), which rejected as 'plainly without substance' an Elections Clause challenge to a referendum on a congressional map.
facts.explanation: The broad claim runs into two on-point precedents, and Kavanaugh joined the 2023 majority. Missouri's narrower version is genuinely open: no case holds that a 5% petition may suspend a map before any statewide vote occurs. The state's brief argues that gap; its public rhetoric argues the broad claim.

corroboration.source: Missouri Supreme Court opinion (collecting Hildebrant, Hawke, AIRC)

facts.claim: The secretary of state delayed his ruling on the referendum petition until the last legally permitted day, which was primary day.
facts.evidence: Opinion, n.8: 'the secretary chose to delay his certification until the last possible day — August 4 — and, in the meantime, utilized the congressional redistricting in HB 1 while incurring the time and expense of signature verification despite having represented to the federal district court he believed the referendum petition was constitutionally deficient.'
facts.explanation: A court finding on stipulated facts, not an advocate's characterization. Von Glahn's brief adds Attorney General Hanaway's radio remark, quoted from the record: 'As long as the status quo is the new maps, delay works in our favor.' The secretary's answer is that he was entitled to the full statutory period, which is true and does not rebut the finding.
facts.source: Missouri Supreme Court, von Glahn v. Hoskins (Sept. 3, 2026), n.8

corroboration.source: von Glahn opposition to stay, No. 26A304

facts.claim: About 1.2 million Missourians voted in the August 2026 primary using the HB 1 districts, and the winners would now run in different ones.
facts.evidence: Application: 'that map was used about one year later in the August 2026 Primary Election, in which about 1.2 million Missourians voted... it undoubtedly will require the winners of the Primary Election to run in dramatically different districts for the General Election.'
facts.explanation: That the primary ran on HB 1 is undisputed by everyone including the state court. The turnout figure comes from the state, a party to the case, and is rounded; no independent tally was located. Von Glahn's answer is not that the harm is imaginary but that the secretary created it by running a primary on a map he knew was unresolved.
facts.source: Emergency application for stay, Hoskins v. von Glahn, No. 26A304

facts.claim: Switching to the 2022 map is impossible in the time remaining and would force Missouri to violate the federal 45-day military-ballot deadline.
facts.evidence: Trial court: 'changing the maps at this late juncture is not just "impractical," it is impossible.' Von Glahn: that finding 'relied only on that former official's affidavit,' while the current Jackson County election directors said publicly, 'We are equipped to make the necessary changes... It will take some work on our end, but we will be ready.'
facts.explanation: The deadline is real: 52 U.S.C. § 20302(a)(8)(A) requires transmitting ballots 'not later than 45 days before the election,' which is September 19. The impossibility is contested, and the evidentiary base on both sides is thin — one former official against current officials in the most-affected county, neither tested by cross-examination.
facts.source: von Glahn opposition to stay, No. 26A304

facts.claim: Justice Kavanaugh's September 8 order decided that Missouri's federal constitutional arguments fail.
facts.evidence: The docket entry reads in full: 'Application (26A304) denied by Justice Kavanaugh.' No opinion issued, no referral to the full Court, no reasoning given.
facts.explanation: A single justice's in-chambers denial of emergency relief is not a merits ruling and creates no precedent; it can rest on jurisdiction, equities, or timing. Both camps have read it as vindication — the referendum's backers as an endorsement of the state court, the state as a mere scheduling loss. Neither reading has a document behind it.
facts.source: U.S. Supreme Court docket, Hoskins v. von Glahn, No. 26A304

facts.claim: The federal restraining order left the secretary no lawful option but to direct counties to use HB 1.
facts.evidence: Clark's order enjoins Hoskins 'from implementing, using, publishing, distributing, or mandating the use of any congressional district map other than the HB 1 map' for November 3. The state injunction restrains him 'from implementing, using, or mandating the use of the congressional redistricting in HB 1.' Chief Justice Powell's show-cause order names a third course: 'take no action in all things related to the congressional district map until guidance is received from a higher court.'
facts.explanation: The conflict is genuine, and the Supremacy Clause argument is not frivolous — a federal injunction binds. But 'no option' is too strong: affirmatively instructing clerks to use HB 1 went beyond refraining, and the standstill the state court identified would have violated neither order. The TRO's text was quoted from reporting, not read directly.
facts.source: Law Dork (quoting the TRO and the state injunction)

facts.claim: The Missouri Supreme Court's ruling was a partisan decision by a court hostile to the map.
facts.evidence: The September 3 opinion ends 'All concur' — unanimous. Fox News notes the seven-member court has 'Five justices appointed by Republican governors.' The same court had already upheld HB 1 against a different challenge in Luther v. Hoskins, 730 S.W.3d 567 (Mo. banc 2026), cited in the state's own application.
facts.explanation: A unanimous, Republican-appointed bench that previously ruled for the map is weak ground for a partisan-court story. It does not make the ruling correct; unanimity is not proof, and the March decision was 4-3. But the composition is checkable and cuts against the framing, which is why it appears in a right-leaning outlet's own account.
facts.source: Missouri Supreme Court, von Glahn v. Hoskins (Sept. 3, 2026)

powerLens.thesis: Nobody in this fight has a durable view about whether a state supreme court gets the last word on state election law; they have a view about which map that word protects. The role-reversed case is four years old and involved the same argument with the parties switched.

precedent.what: New York's Court of Appeals struck down the Democratic legislature's congressional map on April 27, 2022 as an unconstitutional partisan gerrymander enacted in violation of state procedure, handed the redraw to a special master, and forced the primary to be moved to August. Republicans flipped four New York seats that fall.
precedent.mirror: A state high court voided the majority party's congressional map in an election year, on state-constitutional grounds, at enormous administrative cost. Republicans then called it the rule of law and Democrats called it judicial disruption of a running election. In Missouri the identical facts produce the identical arguments from the opposite mouths.
precedent.source: All About Redistricting, Loyola Law School

flips.then: North Carolina's Republican legislative leaders told the Supreme Court in Moore v. Harper that the Elections Clause barred their state supreme court from applying the state constitution to a congressional map. They lost 6-3 in June 2023, Kavanaugh in the majority.
flips.now: Missouri's application argues that the Missouri Constitution's referendum cannot constrain the General Assembly's congressional map — the same structural claim in narrower dress, filed to the justice who voted against it.
flips.source: Brennan Center for Justice (then); Hoskins application (now)

flips.then: On November 4, 2025 California voters passed Proposition 50 by roughly 64-36, suspending the state's independent citizens commission for congressional maps through 2030 so the legislature could draw roughly five additional Democratic seats.
flips.now: The same coalition describes Missouri's mid-decade redraw as an illegitimate power grab. The distinction offered — that California's went to a statewide vote — is real, and it is also the distinction Missouri Republicans are fighting to prevent here.
flips.source: Ballotpedia (via CNN reporting on the result)

powerLens.longRun: Strip the labels and the through-line is that state courts are sovereign expositors of state law exactly when they rule your way, and lawless activists when they do not — and that the losing side's next move is a different courthouse. That predicts the next reversal instead of resolving this one: when a Democratic legislature's map is voided by a Republican-appointed state court in 2028, the briefs will be recycled with the signatures swapped.
powerLens.appliedToScore: Neither side gets a reasoning-honesty credit for institutional principle here; both positions track the seat. The inconsistency sits in each side's weakest point, and the needle rests only on present-tense checkable claims — what the Missouri opinion holds, what Moore v. Harper held, what the record says about the timeline and the ballot deadline.

pattern.thesis: Missouri reads as a bizarre local meltdown only if you look at Missouri. It is the marginal seat in a two-year, nationwide mid-decade redistricting race in which both parties have redrawn maps between censuses, and in which the deciding institution has increasingly been whichever court a party could reach fastest.

campaigns.what: Mid-decade redraw worth about five Republican seats, blocked below, then allowed to take effect after the U.S. Supreme Court stayed the lower-court ruling in December 2025.
Proposition 50 suspended the independent commission for congressional maps through 2030, worth about five Democratic seats; approved roughly 64-36 and upheld in federal court.

Voters approved a Democratic mid-decade amendment worth about four seats; the Supreme Court of Virginia struck it down 4-3 and the existing map stands for 2026 — a state high court voiding a map, with the partisan valence reversed.
A single Republican seat, suspended by referendum petition, restored by a federal restraining order, and now the subject of contempt proceedings against the official who has to administer it.
campaigns.source: Missouri Supreme Court, von Glahn v. Hoskins

pattern.takeaway: The recurring question is whether any neutral rule now governs when maps may be redrawn and who decides — or whether the answer is simply whoever reaches a sympathetic court first. The one-off tell is an account of Missouri that never mentions Texas, California or Virginia.

notAdjudicable: Whether a legislature should be able to redraw congressional districts mid-decade at all — a question about the legitimacy of a practice both parties now use, not about what any statute says.
Whether 3.3% of registered voters signing a petition should be able to suspend a duly enacted law before any vote occurs: that is a judgment about how much friction direct democracy deserves.
Whether the finality of a completed primary outweighs the finality of a state constitution's plain text when the two collide — a ranking of goods, not a factual dispute.
Whether an official who believes a state court order is unconstitutional should comply and appeal, or comply with the order he prefers and accept the contempt risk.
Whether one House seat is worth this much institutional damage — a cost-benefit judgment on which reasonable people weigh the same facts oppositely.
biasWatch: The bias to watch today is court-as-scoreboard: treating each ruling as a point scored rather than as an answer to a specific question, so that four courts answering four different questions reads as chaos or as vindication depending on who you wanted to win. Kavanaugh answered whether to grant emergency relief. Judge Clark answered whether primary voters have a federal claim. The Missouri Supreme Court answered what the Missouri Constitution says. None of them answered whether the map is fair. The tell works on either side: when someone tells you a court 'sided with' Republicans or Democrats, ask what question that court was actually asked. If the answer comes back as a party name rather than a legal question, you are being given a scoreboard, not a ruling.
